Leveraging Large Language Models for Sequential Recommendation

cited_details.statement: Foundation models such as large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced recommender systems because LLMs can formulate diverse recommendation tasks—including rating prediction, sequential recommendation, straightforward recommendation, and explanation generation—into language instructions (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).
This reformulation enables universal recommendation engines that handle heterogeneous tasks through a single natural-language interface (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).

Sequential recommendation aims to predict users' future interactions by modeling collaborative filtering signals drawn from the historical behaviors of similar users or items (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3604915.3610639).

A representative line of work presented at RecSys'23 introduces LLM-based sequential recommenders organized around similarity-based and prompt-based models, labeled LLMSeqSim and LLMSeqPrompt, with hybrid variants named EmbeddingEnsemble, LLMSeqSim&Sequential, and LLMSeqSim&Popularity (https://github.com/dh-r/llm-sequential-recommendation).
Product embeddings are produced through OpenAI utilities and stored for downstream similarity computation (https://github.com/dh-r/llm-sequential-recommendation).

The released code is evaluated on the Beauty dataset and the Delivery Hero dataset, the latter being a food-delivery business service whose public release was under discussion with the organization at the time of the repository (https://github.com/dh-r/llm-sequential-recommendation).

Evaluation pipelines use the SessionDataset abstraction, with metrics such as those enumerated in evaluation.py consuming predicted item rankings against held-out ground truths (https://github.com/dh-r/llm-sequential-recommendation).

Traditional recommender systems operate as "black boxes" that offer limited interactivity and explainability, which constrains their deployment in real-world applications (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).

Chat-REC addresses these limitations through a training-free framework that augments LLMs with conversational recommender capabilities by converting user profiles and historical interactions into natural-language prompts (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).

The framework executes a two-stage decision process: it first determines whether the query requires a recommendation, and if so, it interfaces with a traditional recommender to generate an initial candidate set that the LLM filters and re-ranks via in-context learning (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).

For new items lacking interaction data, Chat-REC exploits the LLM's textual understanding of item descriptions, and for truly novel items, external descriptions are embedded with text-embedding-ada-002 to compute similarity against the query (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).

Experiments on MovieLens 100K report improvements in top-k recommendation and zero-shot rating prediction, measured by Precision, Recall, NDCG, RMSE, and MAE (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).
Cross-domain transfer of user preferences is enabled because preferences are encoded in prompts rather than trained parameters (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).

TALLRec provides an effective and efficient tuning framework that aligns LLMs with recommendation tasks through instruction tuning built atop the Alpaca_lora repository (https://github.com/SAI990323/TALLRec).

The framework reports AUC results in movie and book scenarios, automatically aggregating the results of multiple seeds and sample files into a single output JSON (https://github.com/SAI990323/TALLRec).
A published arXiv version accompanies the repository (https://github.com/SAI990323/TALLRec).

The RecSys 2023 tutorial organizes trustworthy LLM-based recommendation around hallucination, fairness, transparency, robustness, and controllability, and outlines multiple perspectives including data preparation, model design, pre-training, fine-tuning, prompting, evaluation, multi-modality, and multi-task learning (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).

The tutorial highlights OpenP5 as a hands-on platform for designing, pre-training, fine-tuning, prompting, and evaluating LLM-based recommender systems, with T5 and LLaMA identified as common LLM backbones (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a complementary approach to mitigate hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent reasoning by incorporating knowledge from external databases (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997).

RAG enables continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information, and its paradigms have evolved through Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG stages, anchored on a tripartite foundation of retrieval, generation, and augmentation techniques (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997).

Industrial LLM systems that support recommendation functionality include ChatGPT, Microsoft Bing, and Google Bard, which the tutorial identifies as examples that simultaneously illustrate the advantages and the remaining problems of LLM-based recommendation in production (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).

The tutorial also catalogs open-source LLM backbones such as T5 and LLaMA, alongside LLM-based recommendation platforms including OpenP5, as research infrastructure for the field (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).

The sequential recommendation repository notes that the Delivery Hero dataset was being negotiated for public release, constraining reproducibility for that business-service scenario (https://github.com/dh-r/llm-sequential-recommendation).

Chat-REC acknowledges that LLMs inherit knowledge-cutoff limitations, which it mitigates through external information injection rather than eliminating the dependence on a traditional recommender for the initial candidate set (https://www.alphaxiv.org/audio/2303.14524).
The RAG survey delineates outstanding challenges for retrieval-augmented systems without enumerating them in the supplied abstract (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997).

The RecSys 2023 tutorial frames multi-modality, multi-task learning, fairness, transparency, and robustness as open directions for improvement in LLM-based recommendation (https://llmrecsys.github.io/).
